evals.prompt: I run Northbound, a single-track infrastructure conference in Manchester. The CFP just closed: 190 proposals, 22 slots. Six of us organise it and all six can read proposals; we've blocked a two-hour video call in three weeks to decide together. My plan is to have everyone rate each proposal 1 to 5 on overall quality, average the six scores, and take the top 22. The call said we'd review submissions without seeing names. What should the rating sheet look like?
evals.expected_output: A small consensus committee design with the letter-grade advocate scale replacing the proposed numeric average, best-worst pair aggregation, mandatory comments, a cut rule fixed before ranking, a shortlist-stage program-fit pass, and an ordered backup list.
expectations: Recommends the small consensus committee model for this pool, given 190 proposals, six readers and one synchronous discussion round
Replaces the proposed 1-to-5 quality average with the letter-grade advocate scale (A/B/C/D/X), whose grades describe advocacy rather than quality
States that A means the reviewer will actively advocate, B means likes it but will not advocate, C means neutral, and D means will advocate against
Includes an X grade meaning the reviewer abstains because they suspect they have identified the speaker
States that grades aggregate as a best-worst pair per proposal (for example 'AC') and are never averaged
States that at least one A is the practical floor for serious consideration, so a proposal carrying only B, C and D grades cannot get in
Requires a written comment attached to every grade
Instructs writing the rubric down before any scoring begins, and warns that changing the rules once scoring has opened invalidates what was already read
States that the cut rule, as a threshold or a percentage, must be fixed before anyone sees the ranking
Runs the topic, employer and first-timer balance pass on the shortlist rather than on all 190 proposals
Recommends an explicitly ordered backup list, cites about five talks as the documented single-track size, and flags any other number as extrapolation
Does not recommend averaging numeric scores or ranking proposals by mean score

evals.prompt: Kestrel Summit, 310 proposals for 28 slots. Our published call said reviewers would see submitter names and bios - we were explicit about it. Last year we got criticised because 24 of our 26 speakers were men, and two board members now want us to switch this year's review to anonymous, starting Monday when the committee begins reading, to fix the imbalance. They want to announce it as our diversity measure. How do we set it up?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to retrofit anonymization into this edition, an honest statement of what blind review is and is not evidenced to do, the outreach-versus-review distinction, and balance work relocated to a documented shortlist trade.
expectations: Refuses to retrofit anonymization into this edition because the published call promised named review
States that anonymization introduced after reviewers have already read names anonymizes nothing
Treats anonymization as deleted from the menu for this edition rather than demoted or parked as a fallback option
States that no evidence exists that anonymized review changes acceptance outcomes by demographic
Declines to present blind review as a proven or demonstrated equity outcome, describing it instead as a process commitment or mechanism design
Warns against announcing anonymization publicly as the diversity measure
States that under-representation is addressed by outreach before the call closes, not by the review process afterwards
States that a balance goal unsupported by outreach before the call closed can only be traded for at the shortlist stage this year
Says that where the call published named review, the honest path is to run named review and carry the fairness load in the published criteria
Routes the anonymization-policy decision to the next edition's call design rather than deciding it mid-review
Places any balance work in a program-fit pass over the shortlist, with the trade-offs written down
Does not claim a specific percentage improvement in speaker demographics from switching to blind review

evals.prompt: Tidewater Devcon. 240 submissions, 30 slots, four reviewers, and we promised blind review in the call. Our CFP platform has an anonymous review mode and we switched it on, so I think we're covered. One thing: the same submission form also asks whether the speaker needs a travel grant, and we told people that asking wouldn't hurt their chances. It's a fairly tight community, most of us have been to the same meetups for years. Anything else to set up before reviewers start Monday?
evals.expected_output: The documented limit of platform-level hiding, a dedicated anonymizer promoted on the travel-grant and small-community conditions, that role's exact mechanics and its cost, and a written identity re-entry point.
expectations: States that the platform's anonymous mode hides the author field but not identifying details the submitter wrote into the title, abstract or outline
States that this limit must be disclosed to submitters before the call closes rather than discovered during review
Promotes a dedicated anonymizer above platform-level hiding for this event
Keys that promotion to the travel-grant requests riding on the same submission form
Names anonymization as the enforcement mechanism for the promise that requesting financial assistance will not affect a proposal's chances
Assigns the anonymizer role to a named person or people who will not score any proposal
States that the anonymizer rewrites identifying details into bracketed placeholders
States that the anonymizer deliberately preserves identity where it is the subject of the talk itself
States that proposals get random IDs so that submission order cannot re-identify a submitter
Notes that a committee this small may recognise regular submitters regardless of what the tool hides
Names the information loss as the anonymizer's cost: reviewers genuinely see less than under platform-level hiding
Fixes in writing the step at which identity re-enters the process, and for whom

evals.prompt: ScaleFest: 2,100 submissions across four tracks, 96 speaking slots. We have 32 volunteer reviewers who signed up by track, plus me and my co-chair. Two things I want to get right. First the structure - last year everything landed on the two of us and it was a disaster. Second, a board member found that CHI accepts 26.4% of papers and is pushing us to accept at least a quarter of what we got so we don't waste good submissions. And at 2,100 submissions, shouldn't we just add a fifth track?
evals.expected_output: A multi-tier cascade with its documented percentage stages and mandatory comments, the star rubric matched to reviewers who will not meet, the academic acceptance figure rejected as non-transferable, and the track-count question refused and routed elsewhere.
expectations: Recommends the multi-tier cascade for this pool, given four tracks and 2,100 submissions
Describes track committees scoring within their own track as the first tier
States that the top-scoring 30% advance from track committees to track chairs
States that track chairs pass roughly 30% of those on - about 9% of the original pool - to the co-chairs
States that comments are mandatory when track chairs pass proposals up to the co-chairs
Places the final accept decision with the co-chairs, combining committee scores with a program-fit overlay
Recommends the multi-criteria star scale across content, originality, relevance and speaker fit, with mandatory written feedback on every rating, because these reviewers will not all meet
Rejects the 26.4% academic figure as non-transferable, explaining that a peer-reviewed venue accepts what clears a quality bar while a conference fills a fixed number of slots in a room
Treats the resulting acceptance ratio of roughly 96 in 2,100 as an outcome to record rather than a target to hit
Cites a developer-conference calibration point such as PyCon US 2025 selecting about 15% of 938 proposals or KubeCon EU 2024 accepting 9% of 2,541
Refuses to add a fifth track in response to submission volume, stating that a high submission-to-slot ratio is a demand signal and that track count was fixed before the call opened
States that no published reviewers-per-proposal curve exists, and labels any per-proposal reviewer count it proposes as an interpolation

evals.prompt: Quick one, our review opens Thursday. Marisol, one of our seven reviewers, tells me one of the submitters is a senior engineer on her own team - they sit next to each other. She's offering to score it as normal and just put a note in the comment saying she knows him. Separately, another reviewer says he's 90% sure he knows who wrote one of the anonymised proposals from the writing style. And a third reviewer works at a company that competes head-on with three submitters' employers. What's the policy, and what do I do if someone refuses to step back?
evals.expected_output: A conflict-of-interest brief that prescribes abstention rather than score-and-disclose, separates identity suspicion from relationship conflict, admits the honour-system limit, and pre-decides arbitration and the low-coverage fallback.
expectations: Instructs Marisol to abstain from scoring that proposal rather than score it and disclose the connection in a comment
Applies the same abstention rule to the reviewer whose employer competes with submitters' employers
Instructs the reviewer who suspects he has identified an anonymised submitter to abstain on that proposal
Treats identity-suspicion abstention and relationship-based recusal as two distinct failures, both named in the reviewer brief
Notes that one documented model additionally obliges a reviewer with a lesser conflict who continues reviewing to state that conflict in the review text itself
States that the brief must reach reviewers before scoring opens, not after a conflict surfaces
States that conflict-of-interest handling in this field is honour-system self-recusal, with no declared-conflict registry, escalation path or audit mechanism published anywhere
Labels any escalation or arbitration procedure it proposes as the organizer's own design rather than established practice
Names in advance who arbitrates when a reviewer refuses to recuse
Decides in advance what happens to a proposal that loses so many reviewers to recusal that its scores are no longer comparable
Frames reviewing as done wearing the event's hat rather than an employer's

evals.prompt: Harbourline Conf: 340 proposals, 26 slots, decisions are made. I want to get the 314 rejections out tomorrow morning to clear my inbox, then send the acceptances in the afternoon once I've drafted something nicer. For the six people we nearly took, I was going to write "you're first in line, I'd say an 80% chance a slot opens for you." Also Priya got two talks accepted and I'm not sure what to do about that. Can you write the three emails?
evals.expected_output: The notification order reversed, acceptances carrying a confirmation deadline, the waitlist built and ordered first, no probability given to waitlisted speakers, and the duplicate acceptance handed back to the speaker.
expectations: Reverses the proposed order so that acceptances go out before declines
States that declines are sent only once acceptances are confirmed, because a confirmed speaker dropping out would otherwise force retracting a decline
Attaches a confirmation deadline to the acceptance email
States that the confirmation deadline is what makes the waitlist function at all
Refuses to give the waitlisted submitters the 80% figure or any probability of promotion
States that no published data exists on how often a waitlisted talk is actually promoted
Gives waitlisted submitters a specific date by which they will know, in place of odds
Tells waitlisted submitters plainly that a slot may never open
Builds and explicitly orders the waitlist before any notification is sent
Handles Priya's two acceptances by letting her choose which talk to give, or by suggesting a preference, rather than deciding for her
Includes the acceptance arithmetic - 340 proposals for 26 slots - in the decline email
Advises against telling a waitlisted submitter they are first in line or that a slot will definitely open

evals.prompt: Millbrook Devfest is small: 74 proposals, 18 slots, and 41 of the submitters have never spoken at a conference before. Our rubric already forces every reviewer to write a comment alongside their score, so we have text sitting there for everything. My co-organiser wants to send one identical two-line "thanks but no" to all 56 rejections because it's fastest, and where a talk was weak he wants to soften it - say "scheduling constraints" instead of what the reviewers actually said. Which way do we go?
evals.expected_output: Per-proposal feedback promoted above the default rung on its stated conditions, the invented-reason substitution refused, and the three rules that keep written feedback from backfiring.
expectations: Promotes per-proposal written feedback above the default decline rung for this event
Names the promotion conditions met here: a pool small enough to write them all, a first-time-heavy pool, and a rubric that already mandates written comments
States that because the comments already exist, the remaining cost is editorial time rather than writing feedback from scratch
Rejects substituting "scheduling constraints" for what the reviewers actually wrote
States that invented softer reasons produce feedback a speaker cannot act on and will contradict the decision if the speaker follows up
Strips reviewer names and attribution so the feedback reads as coming from the committee rather than from a person
Says plainly to the submitter that the feedback explains this decision in this pool, not a general assessment of them as a speaker
Notes that the default rung is a decline plus a recap of the published criteria including the acceptance ratio
States that the plain identical form decline buys nothing beyond not being silent
States that the acceptance ratio reframes a decline as arithmetic rather than a verdict
Includes an invitation to submit again at the next edition

evals.prompt: We run Cadence, our company's annual user conference. About 20 of the 34 sessions are our own staff plus named industry people we invited months ago; the other 14 come from an open call that just closed with 160 submissions. Our VP of Sales wants two of those 14 open slots given to our two platinum sponsors. Our head of content wants the 20 invited sessions dropped into the same anonymous review as the open pool so it's all fair. What's the right call?
evals.expected_output: Invited sessions kept out of the blind pool with the reason stated, the vendor pole named explicitly against the community-pole rule on sponsor slots, and the promise made to the 160 open submitters protected.
expectations: Refuses to put the 20 invited sessions through blind review alongside the open pool
States that an invited speaker's identity is the reason they were invited, so anonymising it corrupts both the invited lane and the open pool
Requires the invited lane to be decided and written down before review opens
Identifies Cadence as a vendor or user conference rather than a community conference, and says so explicitly
States that at the community pole the rule is that no speaker spots can be bought by sponsors, ever
Says which pole each recommendation assumes wherever the two poles differ
States that the review mechanics still apply to the 14-slot open slice
States that no published sponsored-to-CFP slot ratio exists for vendor conferences
Requires the treatment of sponsor and invited sessions to match what the open call told submitters
Warns that converting open-call slots into sponsor slots after the fact breaks the promise the call made to the 160 submitters
Notes that the program-fit pass at a vendor conference answers to the vendor's narrative as well as the audience's

evals.prompt: Riverbend Summit: 420 submissions, 38 slots, three tracks. The board has told us at least half the speakers must be first-time speakers and at least a quarter must come from end-user companies. I was going to add a "diversity" column to the reviewer scoring sheet, weighted 20%, so it feeds straight into the ranking. Two of our submissions are panels: one has four speakers all from the same consultancy, another has three speakers, all men. And last year the committee swapped a couple of high-scoring talks for spread and nobody wrote down why, which caused a huge argument in January. How do I set this up?
evals.expected_output: Balance targets kept out of the reviewer scoring sheet and moved to a shortlist program-fit pass, the two panel composition rules applied as gates, and every trade recorded.
expectations: Keeps the first-time-speaker and end-user-company targets out of the reviewer scoring sheet and rejects the weighted diversity column
Notes that the documented 50%-new-speaker and 25%-end-user-company targets are event-level aims that appear as a line item in no documented reviewer rubric
Requires deciding before review opens whether each target is a goal or a hard gate
Applies balance at the program-fit pass over the shortlist rather than inside individual proposal scores
States the panel rule that a session with three or more speakers must include at least one speaker who does not identify as a man
Applies that rule to the three-speaker all-men panel submission
States the rule that all panelists may not come from a single organization, and applies it to the four-speaker consultancy panel
Treats both panel composition rules as gates applied at selection rather than as scoring inputs
Requires writing down each trade made in the program-fit pass and the reason for it
Names the cost of an undocumented balance pass: next edition's committee re-litigates it blind and a submitter who asks gets an answer nobody can give
Labels any balance-pass mechanics beyond weighing committee scores and diversity together at the final cut as the organizer's own design rather than documented practice
Records first-time-speaker count, employer spread and local versus out-of-town share in the accepted set against what was promised
